extracted.intended_audience: performers, venue operators, festival organisers, and members of the public interested in the Edinburgh Festival Fringe
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and practical standards for staging, registering and operating shows and venues at the Edinburgh Festival Fringe, including the festival's open-access ethos, venue and pricing models, registration requirements, and values. Useful for performers, promoters and venue operators planning to participate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Open-access / unjuried festival policy
rubrics_metrics.description: The Fringe is an open-access (or "unjuried") performing arts festival, meaning that there is no selection committee, and anyone may participate, with any type of performance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Fringe Society's constitution set the policy of not vetting or censoring shows; what is performed and how it is done is left entirely to each Fringe group. However, participating in the Fringe requires registration, payment of a registration fee, and use of a Fringe venue if you want to be in the official programme. The Society facilitates rather than curates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Registration and use-of-venue requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Participating in the Fringe requires registration, payment of a registration fee, and use of a Fringe venue. Some outdoor spaces also require registration (notably the Royal Mile).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historically the festival charged a registration fee (example given: 2008 registration fee £289.05). Artists who perform outside these auspices may still perform in the city but will not be part of the official Fringe programme.

rubrics_metrics.name: Programme categorisation / sectioning of shows
rubrics_metrics.description: The official Fringe programme categorises shows into sections for theatre, comedy, dance, physical theatre, circus, cabaret, children's shows, musicals, opera, music, spoken word, exhibitions and events.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comedy is noted as the largest section, making up more than one-third of the programme and having the highest public profile; performers should list their show in the appropriate category for audience discovery and marketing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Venue selection criteria for performers
rubrics_metrics.description: From the performers' perspective, the decision on where to perform is typically based on a mixture of cost, location (close proximity to the main Fringe hubs around the university is seen as an advantage), and the philosophy of the venue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Venue philosophy includes whether a venue specialises in amateur, school or college productions versus semi- or wholly-professional work. Performers should consider venue operator type (commercial vs not-for-profit; year-round vs seasonal) and how that aligns with aims and budget.

rubrics_metrics.name: Venue operator / promoter types and models
rubrics_metrics.description: Fringe venues and promoters operate under different business models: the 'Big Four' multi-room commercial operators, modern multi-space operators, free venues (Free Fringe), and Pay What You Want / mixed models.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each model has implications: Big operators often charge hire and market shows widely; Free venues make rooms available for free and rely on donations; PWYW allows advance ticket purchase or paying on exit, letting performers find paying audiences without large marketing spend. Promoter choice affects exposure, costs and audience expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Free venues / Free Fringe model
rubrics_metrics.description: Some promoters make spaces available for free, with audiences making a donation at the end of the show if they have enjoyed it (the Free Fringe model).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This model was set up in response to increasing costs for performers and tends to operate from pubs and clubs. Although 'Free Fringe' originally referred to a particular operation, the term is often used as shorthand for any free venue. Performers using this model must plan for donation-based income and bar-driven footfall.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pay What You Want (PWYW) and mixed pricing models
rubrics_metrics.description: PWYW is a model where punters can 'Buy a ticket in advance to guarantee a seat or Pay What You Want (PWYW) on exit', a mixture of paid and free enabling performers to find paying audiences without risking large marketing spend.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Introduced by specific promoters and adopted in some venues (examples and adopters cited). PWYW has been used successfully by both emerging and established acts and can be combined with limited advance booking to guarantee seats.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ticketing and pricing practices
rubrics_metrics.description: Ticketing at the Fringe involves a central programme and box office run by the Fringe Society, but many venues use their own ticketing systems; offers such as '2 for 1' early-week deals and Half Price Ticket Tents have been used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Issues to consider include commission splits, ticketing reliability (2008 box office failure cited), independent venue offers, and the use of promotions to drive audiences. Performers and venues should plan ticketing strategy and contingency for technical failures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Production scale and venue facilities
rubrics_metrics.description: Venues range from shoestring rooms to 'super-venues' with substantial investment in staging, lighting and sound; some venues operate multiple performance spaces and can host many shows per day.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Production values and technical requirements should match venue capabilities; larger venues enable higher production values but increase costs and may change the artistic tone and audience expectations. Sharing and partitioning of venues influences scheduling and capacity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Street performance and Fringe Street Events
rubrics_metrics.description: Fringe Street Events feature more than 200 street performers and thousands of buskers on the High Street and Mound Precinct; street performers commonly hand out flyers and perform scenes to sell tickets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Performers who want to do street performance should be aware of the High Street as a focal point and any local registration/licensing requirements for outdoor spaces. Street showcases and free events (Fringe Sunday, etc.) provide exposure but may require logistical planning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Festival vision and values
rubrics_metrics.description: The Fringe Society's 2022 vision was 'to give anyone a stage and everyone a seat' with three guiding values: Celebrate performing arts; Be open to all; Look out for each other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These values are intended to guide behaviours and decisions across stakeholders; performers, venues and organisers are expected to uphold them where necessary, shaping inclusion, equality and community practices at the festival.

rubrics_metrics.name: Content freedom and controversy management
rubrics_metrics.description: The freedom to put on any show has led periodically to controversy when tastes in sexual explicitness or religion have been contravened; organisers have defended the festival's role as an open platform while sometimes addressing specific complaints (e.g., censorship of sexual explicitness in certain shows).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Performers should be conscious of potential local sensitivities and the public profile of contentious content; organisers may contact artists for clarification in public disputes. The festival's unjuried nature does not exempt performers from legal or licensing constraints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Awards, recognition and public profile metrics
rubrics_metrics.description: Awards and prizes — notably the Edinburgh Comedy Awards and other festival awards — contribute to a show's public profile and can play a major role in wider recognition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comedy is highlighted as having the highest public profile partly due to such awards. Competing for and gaining awards can lead to transfers to larger venues or further tours; performers seeking career impact may factor award eligibility and publicity into their festival strategy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Financial risks, costs and fair-pay concerns
rubrics_metrics.description: Staging a Fringe show involves financial risk (venue fees, marketing, accommodation); controversies and campaigns (e.g., 'Fair Fringe') have raised concerns about pay and working practices at the festival.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Performers and producers should budget realistically, be aware of venue fee increases, and consider the impact of promoter models on income and pay. Campaigns and media scrutiny around pay may affect reputation and operational choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of temporary and unconventional performance spaces
rubrics_metrics.description: Fringe venues include theatres, church halls, lecture theatres, function rooms, bars, temporary structures (Spiegeltent, Udderbelly), schools, a public toilet, the back of a taxi, buses and even private homes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Producers can exploit unconventional spaces for novelty and audience interest but must consider practicalities (capacity, accessibility, licensing, technical fit) and how a non-traditional space impacts marketing and audience expectations.
